↳ "5 steps to X" gives them a reason to come back

𝟮 Data

𝟯 Templates
↳ Useful beats interesting every time

𝟰 Contrarian takes
↳ Saves become ammunition for future debates

𝟱 Checklists
↳ Actionable beats inspirational

The pattern: save-worthy content solves a future problem. Something the reader will need again when they're back at their desk.

Likes measure how you made someone feel in the moment. Saves measure how useful you'll be tomorrow.

Bottled spirits imports to the US fell from 82.4 million wine gallons in 2012 to 46.9 million in 2023. A 43% decline over 11 years.

As a share of US spirits consumption, bottled imports went from 18% to 8%. Imports lost share continuously across the period, while domestic production grew enough to more than absorb the decline.

Two structural forces drove this. First, format substitution: the categories that grew (RTDs, Cordials, Specialty) are produced and bottled domestically. Second, supply chain economics: bulk imports plus US bottling captures more margin than fully imported bottled product across most price tiers.

The implication for surviving imported bottled brands cuts two ways. The channel is structurally smaller and contracting.

 The importer set is also tighter, with about 60 companies handling the entire Brandy/Vodka/Gin/Cordials import bucket in 2024.

Survivors will have better share of a smaller pool.

The Supreme Court struck down the tariffs in February. But we have new tariffs that went up this morning.

This is now the 4th legal regime in five months and this one may be a “stickier” tariff

The Financially Conflicted Middle [Consumer Sentiment Series] 5 of 5

The Squeeze + the Splurge. This is where it all lands from this series and evaluating the underlying mechanics of cosumer spending. 

The household in the middle is usually mid-40s to mid-50s which are now peak earning years. 

But they’re also still raising kids (they started late) and starting to help aging parents. Gen X is now the biggest-spending generation, and more than half of them are supporting a kid, a parent, or both. 

Peak income and peak obligations at the same time, with inflation widening the gap between them. This is basically the squeeze.

The response is fairly predictable: trade down on everyday things, then spend on one small treat. The “lipstick effect.” About 3 in 4 consumers traded down in at least one category last year, but most still planned to splurge somewhere. 

And the splurging skews young now with roughly 63% being high-income millennials. When the big goals feel out of reach, the small wins are the small reassuring indulgences. And these are not investments in assets but guilty pleasures. 

That’s also what’s behind the vibecession. 

Sentiment is down about 30% year over year, but spending rose 5–6%. Strip out inflation and real spending grew only about 2% — most of that “resilient consumer” is just people paying more for the same stuff. (Kyla Scanlon  coined “vibecession,” though she now says it’s more than just vibes.)

Medical cannabis moved to Schedule III in April. The U.S. Department of Justice is holding expedited hearings on full rescheduling right now.

The Third Space Is Not Coming Back: 

A third place is any space that isn't home and isn't work. The bar. The diner. The bowling alley. The golf club. Sociologist Ray Oldenburg argued in 1989 these aren't amenities. They are the physical infrastructure through which communities maintain themselves.

That infrastructure is contracting. And the data tells us why.
What the numbers show:
- Americans spent 43 minutes per day socializing in 2014. By 2019, before any pandemic, that had already fallen to 38 minutes. By 2024 it sits at 35. No recovery.

- The lost time didn't move to other social activities. It moved to household tasks (+14 min/day), sleeping (+13 min/day), and screens.

- In 2014, Americans watched TV for 3.9 minutes for every 1 minute socializing. By 2023 that ratio was 4.7 to 1.

- Bars and nightclubs lost 1,371 establishments from 2014 to 2023. Annual declines starting four years before COVID.

- Bowling centers down 13%. Golf courses down nearly 400 locations.

- Coffee shops grew 53% in units. Starbucks now runs 70% of sales through drive-thru and mobile. More locations, fewer gathering occasions.

Three Major Attributed Drivers...
- Smartphones (no surprise) optimized for content consumption replaced social exchange. 

- Car-dependent development removed the conditions for incidental gathering. Made worse with the pandemic shut down of pulbic transit and forcing many to purchase vehicles to get to work (seperately, this drove much of the used car market). 

- On-premise economics made the cost of going out hard to justify when the social outcome is available at home for free.

This is not a pandemic story. The behavioral shift was already running at 1.1 minutes per year before 2020. COVID compressed five years of trajectory into eighteen months.

Beer companies are buying spirits brands. Spirits companies are launching canned cocktails. Distributors are laying off hundreds.
Is beverage alcohol still three categories — or is it becoming one?

Molson Coors Beverage Company and Rahul Goyal are not waiting for beer to recover — they're moving into adjacent occasions. The Boston Beer Company has been doing this for years. Campari Group is tightening the portfolio while the category is wide open. Suntory Global Spirits is betting on premiumization as a long cycle, not a short one. AB InBev and Brown-Forman are navigating the same structural pressure from different positions on the board...may even be fully merged into Pernod Ricard

The distributor tier is already consolidating around this reality. Reyes Beverage Group, Republic National Distributing Company, Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits are not building infrastructure for three neat categories. They're building for throughput across occasions.

The three-tier system was designed for a world where beer, wine, and spirits were distinct. That world is going away. The consumer has already moved — ready-to-drink, hard seltzer, canned cocktail, non-alc. The channel is following. The supplier tier is the last one still debating categories as if they're fixed.

Distillery Starts vs Stops: 9 distillery closures in 2012. 123 in 2024. A 13x increase in 12 years, in a regulatory category where shutting down requires actively surrendering a federal permit.

The growth in closures has compounded steadily, not in a single bad year. 35 closures in 2018. 75 in 2021. 123 in 2024. The trend line is unambiguous.

The issuance side has stayed remarkably stable across the same period. 350 to 500 new permits per year, every year, since 2012. Net additions are still positive only because of delta: 411 new entrants in 2024 minus 123 closures gives 288 net.

Project that forward. If closures continue compounding at the current rate and issuance holds steady, net additions turn negative inside 36 months.

So What Is the Top Actually Buying?

Half of all consumer spending now comes from the top 10%. So  what are they buying?

Big stuff…and a very specific kind of big-ticket.

Federal Reserve Bank of New York  (Liberty Street Economics — Chakrabarti & Pham) tracked real spending growth by income since 2023. 

The split is not reassuring. 

- Low earners (under $40K): +1%
- Middle: +3%
- High earners (over $125K): +7.6%

Look at “recreational goods and vehicles” the Bureau of Economic Analysis polite term for boats, RVs, motorcycles, e-bikes, high-end gear. Basically, expensive toys. 

Real spending in that one category went from about $654B in 2021 to $819B in 2025. That’s +25% in real terms… while overall real spending barely budged.

Add the rest of the durable good like new cars, furnishings, jewelry, watches + luxury goods, high-end dining and entertainment, and you’ve got the actual shape of “the resilient consumer.” 

It’s actually a discretionary, big-ticket, top-heavy story.

Issue is durable and toys are the most cancellable category in the entire economy. Nobody NEEDS a new boat (though we would all like one). That spending only happens when people feel rich and people only feel rich when their assets are up.

We are not looking at a sturdy consumer.

Data: New York Fed (Liberty Street Economics), U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The Financially Conflicted Middle [Consumer Sentiment Series] 1 of 5

What the heck is Middle?

First, there is no formal definition. Almost no one agrees on what “the middle class” actually means. Especially politicians…

Pew Research Center arguably has the best definition of “middle-income” households as those earning between two-thirds and double the national median, adjusted for household size thats roughly $57,000 to $170,000 for a household of three. By that definition, about half of American households qualify.

That half, used to be a very clear majority in 1971. 61% of U.S. households were middle-income. 

Forward to 2023, it was 51%. 

The middle has thinned out over five decades  with some households moving up but WAY more feeling left behind (just look at recent consumer sentiment)

But there is more to it. The bigger problem is that “middle-income” no longer tells you whether someone feels middle class. 

Two households can earn the exact same paycheck and live in completely different economies and the other underwater. Income is just the first tollgate in the conversation. 

That gap between what the middle earns and how the middle feels is the whole point of what I am going to attempt to convey. Started as a deep dive for work but is worth breaking up and sharing. 

Over the next four posts I’ll get into where it actually comes from: assets, age, timing, and behavior.

The most commonly cited growth statistic in US spirits gets misread.
7.5x growth in active distillery permits from 2012 to 2024 reads as a boom. The mechanism that produced it is not what a boom looks like.

New permit issuance has held steady at 350 to 500 per year for the entire decade. Issuance didn't accelerate. The base compounded because closures stayed near zero.

That distinction matters....acceleration would show as a curve bending upward. This curve is a flat line of new entrants laid on top of a base that kept growing because almost nobody left.

Steady issuance plus near zero attrition is what late stage market expansion looks like in any industry. The 12 year curve is dramatic because of math, not because of velocity.
